title: The Meyer and Anna Prentis Family Foundation, Inc. v. Barbara Ann Karmanos Cancer Institute
lead: A family foundation contributed a cancer-research endowment under an agreement recognizing the Prentis name, then sued after a merger and later donor led to renaming. Michigan’s Court of Appeals rejected the foundation’s naming-contract and standing theories and upheld dismissal of its claims against the institution’s lawyers.

actors.name: Meyer and Anna Prentis Family Foundation
actors.role: Charitable donor seeking enforcement of the naming undertaking.

actors.name: Wayne State University
actors.role: Recipient of the endowment installments and party to the agreement.

actors.name: Barbara Ann Karmanos Cancer Institute
actors.role: Defendant institution following the merger and renaming.

actors.name: Honigman, Miller, Schwartz and Cohn
actors.role: Law firm, abbreviated HMSC, sued over its role in the transactions.

proceedings: Foundation appealed dismissal of HMSC and its damages claim; Institute cross-appealed the breach determination. Court of Appeals unanimously affirmed in part and reversed in part, with no express remand instruction.
limits: Slip pinpoints refer to the archived thirteen-page court opinion. Donor standing and contract interpretation are distinct historical rulings; the decision is not a universal rule against charitable naming agreements or nonprofit damages.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The donor creates a fund and receives a naming undertaking
sections.cue: The text later becomes decisive to the claimed exchange.
paragraphs: In 1985 the Meyer and Anna Prentis Family Foundation entered an endowment agreement for a $1.5 million fund payable to Wayne State University in installments of at least $300,000 annually over no more than five years, beginning that year. The fund was restricted exclusively to cancer research. The assigned account states that payments were completed in 1990.

Another provision recognized the Foundation’s longstanding leadership and financial contributions and expressed appreciation for the new fund. The University, the cancer center, and the Michigan Cancer Foundation agreed to rename the center the Meyer L. Prentis Comprehensive Cancer Center of Metropolitan Detroit.

The Michigan Cancer Foundation later merged with the center. The Prentis Foundation’s board representative attended merger discussions in 1994 and discussions and voting about the Karmanos gift and renaming in 1995. On July 27, 2000 the Foundation sued the Barbara Ann Karmanos Cancer Institute and the law firm Honigman, Miller, Schwartz and Cohn, known as HMSC. It alleged breach of the naming undertaking and challenged the lawyers’ role in the original transaction, failure to legally change the name, merger, and later donor arrangement. Wayne State’s role in the agreement did not make it an appellee in this case.

sections.title: The trial proceedings leave several distinct appellate disputes
sections.cue: Legal damages and equitable findings follow different paths.
paragraphs: The Foundation appealed dismissal of HMSC and dismissal of its legal damages claim against the Institute. The Institute separately appealed the determination that it had breached the naming agreement. The Court of Appeals issued a unanimous per curiam decision by Judges Markey, Fitzgerald, and Owens.

The Foundation argued that the trial court could not revise an earlier ruling or require a jury decision on legal liability after a bench trial on equitable matters. The appellate court distinguished an appellate law-of-the-case ruling from a trial judge’s revisable decision. Equitable factfinding did not replace jury factfinding on damages claims. The Institute could rely on the Foundation’s jury demand without making another demand. There was no demonstrated waiver: the pretrial order contemplated a bench trial followed by a jury trial, and the judge’s comments left legal liability for the jury.

Dismissal of damages also stood. The first judge had rejected rescission and related restitution; the later summary-disposition ruling found no demonstrated measurement method and regarded the alleged loss as speculative. Although a jury generally determines amount, the court determines legal entitlement. The Foundation cited no supporting authority for its appellate damages theory, and the court declined to construct one.

sections.title: The Institute prevails on donor standing and the naming provision
sections.cue: The enforceable research restriction was not shown to have been violated.
paragraphs: On the Institute’s cross-appeal, the court applied Michigan’s then-governing standing requirements of concrete injury to a legally protected interest, causation, and likely redressability. A charitable donation created a charitable trust regardless of the donor’s motive, and cancer research was charitable. The Attorney General, a co-trustee, or someone with a special interest could enforce such a trust, but the settlor or heirs could not do so merely in that capacity. The Foundation lacked standing on that basis.

Separately, the court reviewed the unambiguous agreement de novo. Consideration required a bargained exchange involving benefit or detriment. Earlier years of contributions could not support a later promise. The clause’s treatment of the newly created fund still spoke in terms of recognition and appreciation, rather than exchanging payment for the naming promise. The court regarded the naming undertaking as gratuitous and unenforceable. The Foundation’s unilateral expectations could not rewrite the agreement; it could have expressly required return of the funds if the name did not change but had not done so.

The trial court also erred in finding breach. The enforceable obligation restricted the money to cancer research, and nothing showed misuse. Once the naming provision was unenforceable, renaming did not establish breach of the remaining obligation. This interpretation concerned the particular document, not every charitable naming commitment.

sections.title: The lawyers owed duties to the institution, not automatically to its donor
sections.cue: The evidence does not establish the alleged concealed representation.
paragraphs: The Foundation claimed that reasonable reliance created fiduciary duties even without a formal retainer. The court found that its representative’s board service did not establish such a relationship. Corporate counsel represents the corporation, not its shareholders or agents. The Foundation wanted to memorialize a family name, while the center wanted cancer-research funding; their interests were not completely identical. No identified action showed independent representation of the Foundation, and the firm’s agency agreement with the center created no third-party rights. Duties of loyalty, good faith, and avoiding self-dealing owed to the center did not become duties owed to the Foundation.

The record also failed to support concealment and dual-representation allegations. HMSC produced letters disclosing a potential conflict over the Karmanos gift and obtaining consent. A 1993 letter alerted the Foundation’s board representative to a prospective donor receiving name recognition. For the merger, the firm obtained approvals and advised the center to consider independent counsel. A firm lawyer’s signature on merger documents as board chairman did not itself establish legal representation of both parties. The Foundation produced no board minutes showing that lawyer’s participation in the approval decision, and contemporaneous documents reflected discussion of the naming obligation.

sections.title: Limitations and procedural defects supply additional grounds
sections.cue: The final judgment partly affirms and partly reverses.
paragraphs: The fiduciary-duty claim was also untimely. The court rejected HMSC’s proposed two-year malpractice period and applied the three-year period for the alleged tort injury, including lost naming rights. The board representative’s participation meant the Foundation should have known of a possible claim by 1995, more than three years before suit. Fraudulent-concealment tolling required affirmative concealment rather than silence. Accessible public records, absence of a fiduciary relationship, and lack of reasonable investigation defeated tolling. This was additional to the failure to establish an independent duty.

HMSC’s sanctions request failed as well. Trial-level sanctions were not properly before the appellate court without a cross-appeal. Appellate sanctions required a separate motion, not a request in a brief, and appropriate supporting authority was missing.

The judgment was affirmed in part and reversed in part. The Foundation’s challenges failed, while the Institute prevailed on standing, consideration, and breach. The court issued no express remand instruction and no judge wrote separately.
